title: Arrays, memory and pointers
subtitle: Memory is a long row of numbered boxes. An array is a run of them; a pointer is a box that holds a box’s number.

arr.title: Arrays
arr.body: int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; reserves 5 consecutive ints. Indexes run 0 to 4; a[5] is out of bounds and C does not check — it silently reads or corrupts neighbouring memory. Initialise, then process with a loop.

addr.title: Addresses: memory picture
addr.body: Each byte has an address. &x is the address of x. An int array of 4 elements occupies 16 bytes; element i lives at base + 4·i. So the name a itself acts as the address of a[0].
addr.steps: Base address 1000, 4-byte ints. Address of a[3]: base + 3 × 4.

ptr.title: Pointers
ptr.body: int *p = &x; — p stores x’s address; *p (dereference) means “the thing p points to”. *p = 9 changes x. A pointer must be initialised before use; a NULL pointer points nowhere. Pointer arithmetic scales by the element size: p + 1 moves to the next int.

byref.title: Pointers and function arguments
byref.body: C passes arguments by value — a function gets copies. To let a function change the caller’s variable, pass its address: swap(&x, &y) with void swap(int *a, int *b). Arrays are passed as the address of their first element, so a function can modify them.

str.title: Strings
str.body: A C string is a char array ending with the null character '\0': "hi" occupies 3 bytes (h, i, \0). strlen counts up to, not including, the null. Forgetting room for the terminator is a classic overflow.
str.steps: How many bytes does char s[] = "hello"; take? 5 letters + 1 null.

dyn.title: Dynamic memory
dyn.body: malloc(n) asks the heap for n bytes and returns a pointer; free(p) gives it back. Forgetting to free leaks memory; using memory after freeing (dangling pointer) or freeing twice is undefined. Pair every malloc with one free.
